Choosing a Legal Structure

When someone starts a business, one of the first decisions they face is how the business will be legally structured. This is not just administrative paperwork — the chosen structure determines who bears the financial risk, who controls the business, how profits are shared and how much it costs to set up. Getting it wrong can be costly later, so most entrepreneurs think carefully about structure from the start.

The most important concept that runs through all ownership types is unlimited liability. Under unlimited liability, the law treats the owner and the business as the same entity. If the business cannot pay its debts, the owner must pay them from their personal assets — including savings, a car or even a home. This is the greatest financial risk of certain ownership structures.

The opposite is limited liability. Under limited liability, the law treats the business as a separate legal entity from its owners. If the business fails, shareholders only lose what they put in — their personal possessions are safe. This protection makes limited liability structures attractive for any entrepreneur who is investing significant money or taking on meaningful risk.

Key Fact

Unlimited liability — a sole trader and general partners in a standard partnership are personally responsible for all business debts. Limited liability — shareholders in a private limited company (Ltd) and members of a limited liability partnership (LLP) can only lose what they invested. Examiners specifically test whether students know which structure gives which protection — writing “limited responsibility” instead of “limited liability” will cost marks.

The Four Ownership Types (Plus Franchise)

A sole trader is the simplest form of business ownership. There is no formal registration process beyond informing tax authorities. The owner makes all decisions, keeps all the profit after tax and has complete control. This suits independent tradespeople, personal trainers, freelancers and market traders who want flexibility and minimal administration.

The main disadvantages are unlimited liability — every business debt is a personal debt — and limited access to finance, since banks see sole traders as higher risk. If the owner becomes ill or is absent, the business may stop completely. There is also no one to share the workload or contribute complementary skills.

A partnership allows two or more people to go into business together, pooling their skills, experience and start-up capital. A furniture designer and a skilled carpenter, for example, might form a partnership that combines creative and craft expertise neither has alone. Partners share the workload, which can help a business grow faster than a sole trader could manage.

However, standard partners share unlimited liability. If one partner makes a poor business decision that creates a large debt, all partners are personally responsible — even if they had no involvement in that decision. A formal written partnership agreement, setting out each person’s role, decision-making rights and profit share, is strongly recommended to reduce disputes.

A limited liability partnership (LLP) is a variation that gives members the flexibility of a partnership while providing limited liability. This means members’ personal assets are protected if the business cannot pay its debts. LLPs are more common in professional services — law firms and accountancy practices, for example — but are an option available to any start-up that wants the combined skills of a partnership with the financial protection of limited liability.

A private limited company (Ltd) is legally separate from its owners. Shareholders invest in the company and have limited liability — they can only lose the money they put in. This structure requires formal registration with Companies House, and annual accounts are filed publicly. The administration is more complex and costly than a sole trader or partnership.

The advantages are significant: limited liability protects investors, capital can be raised by selling shares to trusted individuals, and the business continues to exist even if a founder leaves or dies. Shares in a private limited company cannot be sold on a stock exchange — they can only be transferred to buyers the existing shareholders approve. This keeps control within a trusted group, which many small business founders prefer.

A franchise is not a legal ownership structure in the same way as sole trader or Ltd — it describes a business operating model. A franchisee buys the right to trade under an established brand and follow a proven system. The advantage is significantly lower risk than starting from scratch: the brand is known, the product or service is tested, and the franchisor provides training and support.

The costs are real, however. The franchisee pays an upfront fee and ongoing royalties — typically a percentage of revenue — to the franchisor. They must follow the franchisor’s rules on pricing, branding and operations. This means the franchisee has far less independence than a sole trader or partner. For someone who wants to run their own business but values the security of a proven model, a franchise can be an attractive route into enterprise.

Key Fact

Sole trader: one owner, unlimited liability, full control, easy to set up. Partnership: shared skills and capital, unlimited liability, risk of disagreement. LLP: partnership flexibility, limited liability for members. Private limited company (Ltd): limited liability, separate legal entity, more administration. Franchise: proven model, lower risk, but less independence and ongoing royalty costs.

Six Sources of Start-Up Capital

Whatever structure a new business adopts, it needs money to get started. This money — called capital — can come from several sources. There are six sources to know.

  • Own savings — using personal savings avoids debt and interest costs. The entrepreneur keeps full control and all future profit. The risk is personal — if the business fails, the savings are lost.
  • Friends and family — money from people close to the entrepreneur can come as a gift (with no repayment obligation) or as an informal loan. This is often faster and easier to arrange than bank finance, but mixing money and personal relationships can create tension if the business struggles.
  • Loans — a bank or financial institution lends a fixed sum that must be repaid with interest over an agreed period. A loan provides a lump sum without giving away ownership of the business, but the obligation to make repayments continues even if sales are low. Note: the loan repayment itself is not classed as a business cost — only the interest on the loan is a cost.
  • Crowdfunding — the entrepreneur pitches the idea on an online platform and many individuals each contribute a small amount. In return, backers may receive an early product, a reward, or (in equity crowdfunding) a small share of the business. Crowdfunding can also generate publicity and test whether there is genuine demand before the product is made.
  • Grants — government bodies, local authorities and some other organisations offer grants to businesses that meet certain criteria, such as being in a specific industry or location. Unlike loans, grants do not have to be repaid, but they are competitive, often come with conditions on how the money is spent, and are not guaranteed.
  • Business angels — wealthy private investors who provide capital in exchange for a share of the business and often an active role as a mentor or advisor. A business angel brings not just money but contacts, experience and guidance. The entrepreneur gives up some ownership and must share future profits and decision-making authority.

Choosing the right source depends on how much capital is needed, how quickly it is needed, how much control the entrepreneur is willing to give up and what obligations come with the money.

Why Do New Business Owners Need Support?

Starting a business is rarely a solo journey. Most new entrepreneurs encounter questions they cannot answer alone — how to manage accounts, whether a contract is legally sound, how to apply for funding, or how to find other local businesses to learn from. Knowing where to find the right help, at the right moment, can be the difference between a business that survives its first year and one that fails through avoidable mistakes.

The kind of support a start-up needs changes at different stages. In the early days, the focus is often on finance and legal structure. Later, it might be about finding customers or managing staff. The key skill — and what this lesson explores — is matching the right type of support to the right problem.

Sources of Support

There are several different categories of support available to a new business. Some provide money, some provide expertise, some provide community and connections, and some provide practical services. A smart entrepreneur draws on more than one.

A bank can provide a range of financial products to a new business: loans to fund start-up costs, business current accounts for day-to-day transactions, and access to financial advice. Banks typically want evidence that the business has a credible plan and a realistic chance of repaying any money borrowed. For a brand-new business with no trading history, getting finance from a bank can be challenging — which is why many entrepreneurs combine bank support with other sources.

A business angel is a private investor who provides capital in exchange for a share of the business and often a seat at the table as a mentor or advisor. Beyond the money itself, a business angel typically brings industry experience, a network of useful contacts, and a genuine stake in seeing the business succeed. This can be especially valuable for a start-up whose founder has a great idea but limited business experience.

The government provides a range of support for new businesses through national schemes and programmes. This can include grants (money that does not need to be repaid), information and guidance on starting up, and training or mentoring schemes. Government support is typically targeted at specific types of business, industries or locations, so a new enterprise must check whether it qualifies before applying.

A local council enterprise department often offers support that is specifically tailored to businesses in that area. This might include help with finding suitable premises, advice on local business rates, introductions to other local businesses, and information about area-specific grants or regeneration funding. Local support tends to be more accessible for a brand-new small business than national programmes, which may be more competitive.

An accountant helps a new business keep on top of its finances. For a start-up, this typically includes setting up bookkeeping systems, preparing tax returns, making sure the business meets its legal obligations to report income, and advising on whether the business is generating profit or heading towards difficulty. Many sole traders and small partnerships use an accountant even if they could manage some of these tasks themselves, simply because professional financial management reduces costly errors.

A solicitor is a legal expert. A new business may need a solicitor to draft or review contracts, register a trademark, advise on the legal structure of a partnership or company, or handle any dispute with a supplier or customer. Legal mistakes are often expensive — a poorly written contract, for example, could leave the business without recourse if a major customer refuses to pay. Using a solicitor early to set up the right legal foundations is often cheaper than dealing with problems later.

Friends and family can be a source of informal support that goes well beyond money. A family member with marketing experience might help with social media. A friend who has set up their own business might share practical advice about what worked and what did not. This informal network is often the first port of call for a new entrepreneur and should not be underestimated.

The Chamber of Commerce is a membership organisation for local businesses. Joining gives access to networking events where entrepreneurs can meet potential customers, suppliers and partners. The Chamber often provides training sessions, business advice workshops and a collective voice to advocate for local business interests to the council or government. For a new start-up looking to build its local network quickly, the Chamber of Commerce can be a genuinely practical resource.

Charitable organisations exist in most parts of the UK to support new or struggling businesses, particularly those run by people from disadvantaged backgrounds or those operating in areas of economic need. Charitable support might include free or subsidised business mentoring, access to shared workspace, help with writing a business plan, or connections to grant funding. Unlike banks, charities are not looking for a financial return, so the support they provide is often more accessible for an early-stage business that has not yet proven its viability.

Key Fact

Eight categories of support for a new enterprise: finance providers, such as banks and business angels (capital, advice and contacts), government (grants and guidance schemes), local council enterprise department (local premises, rates and area-specific funding), accountant (financial management and tax), solicitor (contracts and legal structure), friends and family (informal advice and support), Chamber of Commerce (networking and training), and charities (mentoring and accessible support for early-stage businesses).

Choosing the Right Support

The analytical skill that examiners reward is not just listing sources of support — it is matching the right support to the right situation. Consider three different entrepreneurs:

  • Kezia is starting a food business but has no experience of bookkeeping or tax returns. An accountant is the most directly useful professional for her at this stage, before mistakes accumulate.
  • Marcus is a young entrepreneur with a strong product idea but no industry contacts and limited business experience. A business angel would provide both capital and the mentoring he needs to avoid common pitfalls — at the cost of giving up some ownership.
  • Priya wants to rent a workshop in her town and is looking for local grants. A local council enterprise department is the most targeted starting point, since they hold information about local premises and area-specific funding that national sources would not know about.

In each case, the most appropriate source of support depends on the specific challenge the entrepreneur is facing. A high-mark answer in an exam will always connect the type of support to the entrepreneur’s situation explicitly.

The R067 spec assesses your ability to match support to a specific situation. Identify the entrepreneur's biggest current problem first (cash, legal, premises, expertise), then pick the support source that solves that exact problem.
